endorsements.title: 45 CFR 92.210, nondiscrimination in the use of patient care decision support tools
endorsements.issuer: US Department of Health and Human Services
endorsements.quote: A covered entity has an ongoing duty to make reasonable efforts to identify uses of patient care decision support tools in its health programs or activities that employ input variables or factors that measure race, color, national origin, sex, age, or disability.

evidence.title: Awareness of Racial and Ethnic Bias and Potential Solutions to Address Bias With Use of Health Care Algorithms
evidence.outcome: Identification of algorithms using race or ethnicity as inputs with potential for bias
evidence.effect: Forty-two respondents identified 18 algorithms currently in use with the potential for bias, e.g., SCORE osteoporosis tool and VBAC risk calculator.
evidence.quote: Forty-two respondents identified 18 algorithms currently in use with the potential for bias, including, for example, the Simple Calculated Osteoporosis Risk Estimation risk prediction tool and the risk calculator for vaginal birth after cesarean section.
evidence.sample_unit: respondents to request for information (organization representatives and individuals)

commentary.bottom_line: Federal regulation at 45 CFR 92.210 requires covered entities to make ongoing, reasonable efforts to identify decision support tools that use protected characteristics as inputs, and no study has tested whether such a process detects or prevents discriminatory decisions. One qualitative request-for-information study found 18 algorithms in current use that respondents flagged for potential bias from race or ethnicity inputs.

perspectives.view: No study evaluates an identification process, so certainty for the practice rests on no direct evidence. The one related study is a level 4 qualitative request for information with 42 respondents. It shows that race-based algorithms are in use, but it does not measure how often an inventory finds them or whether finding them changes decisions.

The practice is a legal duty for covered entities under 45 CFR 92.210, so adoption does not depend on evidence of effect. The rule sets a reasonable-efforts standard across six characteristics. The algorithms flagged in the study, such as the SCORE osteoporosis tool and the VBAC risk calculator, suggest the rule may reach ordinary clinical calculators as well as vendor AI products.

The study documents that tools with race or ethnicity inputs remain in clinical use, which is the precondition for discriminatory output going unnoticed. An inventory functions as a detection step and does not by itself correct a biased tool. No evidence shows how many such tools an internal process catches or whether review and correction follow.

The hazard study focused on racial and ethnic minority populations and on race or ethnicity inputs. It did not examine national origin, disability, age, or sex inputs, and it did not report findings from Medicaid or safety-net settings. The available evidence therefore addresses only part of what the rule asks entities to identify.

commentary.research_gap: No study has measured whether an ongoing identification process finds decision support tools that use protected characteristics, how complete its findings are compared with an independent audit, what staff time it requires, or whether identification leads to changes in tool use and patient outcomes. Future work should also cover inputs beyond race and ethnicity, including disability, age, sex, and national origin.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The single hazard study focused on racial and ethnic minority populations, which leaves systems serving these groups without evidence on how well an identification process performs in their settings or for inputs such as national origin that may relate to language access.
